prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought optical timekeeping to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: I change my preferred configuration from B057 to B027. In round 1 I put B057 first because it combined a model-level theoretical idea with a clean quantitative experiment. After the full exchange, two things moved me. First, the credit problem in B057 has not been answered. Eriksson, Olsson and Johansson all name the same gap: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's experiment tested, Zhang is deceased, and the three-dimensional work (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore and Balents; Hasan) is outside the trio. Eriksson, my fellow supporter, has said he would move to the clock if that question stays open. I still think the 2016 overlap is answerable, since band topology of real time-reversal-invariant insulators is not the same thing as topological phases in model systems. But two open questions are one too many for a prize that must be sure of its names. Second, B027 turns out to be the kind of result I trust most. The magic-wavelength condition is a simple and general mechanism: choose the lattice wavelength so that the light shifts of the two clock states cancel. That is a clean idea that can be analysed exactly. It has been reproduced at the 1e-18 level by independent laboratories, and it is understood well enough that systematic shifts can be budgeted. The credit is also the cleanest on the list. Katori proposed the scheme and built the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group took the accuracy to its present level and opened up many-body clock physics. I would word the citation as invention and development so that it does not read as a second-best-experiment prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty relative to the 2005 (comb) and 2012 (single-quantum-system control) prizes, which Johansson calls the deciding issue. I read it as a real concern that does not decide the matter, because neither of those prizes covers neutral atoms held in a lattice with cancelled light shifts. Danielsson's point is also fair: so far the clock has delivered tighter bounds and millimetre-scale redshift tests rather than a surprise. And the SI second has not been redefined. Finally, if Ye is credited for development rather than invention, someone could argue that Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde or Oates should be added. By giving up B057 I also set aside a topological discovery whose conceptual content is larger than the clock's, and I have not resolved the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang question; I have only decided that B027 is easier to defend.

responses.point: Holds B057 first as a new organising principle, answers the 2016 overlap by distinguishing model systems from real band insulators, and says he would move the clock to the top if the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang question stays unsettled.
responses.response: I made your argument about 2016 myself in round 1 and I still think it is right. But your own conditional is the one that decides it for me. The sequence you set out (Kane and Mele 2005, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang 2006, Konig and Molenkamp 2007) shows the HgTe prediction is what the experiment tested, and neither of us has an answer within the three-name limit. I therefore take you up on the offer to move the clock to the top, and I ask you to consider the same. If the committee wished to reward topological insulators in a later year, the same question would need a real answer then, not only a citation worded around it.

responses.point: Moved to B027 and asks whether Ye's contribution is original invention or decisive development, and whether the citation should say which; she also warns against resting the citation on promised applications such as geodesy and dark-matter searches.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The magic-wavelength scheme is Katori's idea, and that is where a prize for invention should rest, so I would keep his name firm. Ye's claim is the demonstration of record accuracy and the many-body clock physics, which is development, and the citation should say 'invention and development' so that it is plain. On your second point, my proposed wording names the demonstrated 1e-18 level rather than geodesy or dark-matter searches, which are not yet results. I do not think the Takamoto, Ludlow or Lemonde contributions are strong enough to disturb a two-name credit, though I am not an atomic physicist and would defer to Lindroth and Kroll on the early record.

responses.point: Argues that cancelling light shifts via the magic wavelength is itself the discovery, that the 2005 and 2012 prizes made the clock possible without covering neutral atoms in a lattice, and that the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice and its accuracy.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me, because it describes a mechanism and not just a technique. I accept that the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is the deciding issue, and I think your answer is right: the comb and ion-control prizes do not contain the lattice-and-magic-wavelength idea. I also agree with you against widening the credit to Zoller. It would blur a clean pair, and Zoller already appears in B060 and B006. On the redefinition of the second, I agree that the prize should be for the invention and demonstrated accuracy, not for the redefinition.

responses.point: Moved to B027 but wants the wording to rest on what the precision has shown, such as redshift tests and many-body clock physics, and observes that a capability is not the same as an answer to a question about nature.
responses.response: I take this seriously as a standard for the citation. The magic-wavelength condition is a statement about atomic structure that can be tested directly, and millimetre-scale redshift tests and the many-body physics in the lattice are results, not promises. I am not sure a short citation can carry all of that. I think 'invention and development' with the 1e-18 level is the honest summary and that the fuller case belongs in the written background.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's role is judged invention or decisive development, and whether Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde or Oates have an attribution claim strong enough to change the two-name credit; I am a theorist outside atomic physics and rely on Lindroth and Kroll here.
Whether the committee sees the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I judge that it is, but not with certainty.
Whether a prize before the redefinition of the second is premature; I think the science is established, but this is a timing judgement.
Whether the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and three-dimensional credit problem in B057 could be solved by a different configuration; I have not found one within the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no collaboration with Katori, Ye or any person credited on B027, B057 or B008. I am in the Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson at Chalmers, but I have no shared work with either of them.
